## Advanced dynamics solutions

### Delay differential equations

#### Solution to Exercise 1 {#solution-a01-ex1}

The exercise asks for the DDE peak and its timing at $\tau \in \{2, 4, 8\}$
(holding $\beta$, $c$, $N$ fixed), compared with the exponential-recovery
ODE at the matching mean infectious period $1/\gamma = \tau$.

```{julia}
#| label: code-sol-a01-ex1
using DelayDiffEq
using OrdinaryDiffEq

function sir_dde!(du, u, h, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    β, c, τ = p
    N = S + I + R
    λ = β * c * I / N
    Sd, Id, Rd = h(p, t - τ)
    Nd = Sd + Id + Rd
    λd = β * c * Id / Nd
    du[1] = -λ * S
    du[2] = λ * S - λd * Sd
    du[3] = λd * Sd
    return nothing
end
sir_history(p, t) = [1000.0, 0.0, 0.0]

function sir_ode_a01ex1!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    β, c, γrate = p
    N = S + I + R
    λ = β * c * I / N
    du[1] = -λ * S
    du[2] = λ * S - γrate * I
    du[3] = γrate * I
    return nothing
end

u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]
tspan = (0.0, 40.0)
results = NamedTuple[]
for τ in (2.0, 4.0, 8.0)
    p = (0.05, 10.0, τ)
    sol_dde = solve(DDEProblem(sir_dde!, u0, sir_history, tspan, p; constant_lags = [τ]),
                     MethodOfSteps(Tsit5()); reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)
    peak_dde, idx_dde = findmax(sol_dde[2, :])

    sol_ode = solve(ODEProblem(sir_ode_a01ex1!, u0, tspan, (0.05, 10.0, 1 / τ)), Tsit5();
                     reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)
    peak_ode, idx_ode = findmax(sol_ode[2, :])

    push!(results, (τ = τ, dde_peak = round(peak_dde; digits = 1), dde_t = round(sol_dde.t[idx_dde]; digits = 2),
                     ode_peak = round(peak_ode; digits = 1), ode_t = round(sol_ode.t[idx_ode]; digits = 2)))
end
results
```

At $\tau = 2$ ($\gamma = 0.5$), $R_0 = \beta c / \gamma = 1.0$ exactly, so the
exponential-recovery ODE cannot grow at all — its "peak" is simply $I(0)=10$
at $t=0$ — while the fixed-delay DDE still produces a modest outbreak,
because every one of the initial infections transmits at full strength for
the entire interval $[0, 2)$ before recovering, rather than a fraction of
them recovering almost immediately. As $\tau$ grows, both the absolute size
of the gap between the DDE and ODE peaks and its relative size increase, and
the DDE peak occurs earlier relative to the ODE peak: the ODE's exponential
recovery spreads recoveries out over a long right tail, so it takes longer
for the ODE epidemic to reach its own (smaller) peak, while the fixed-delay
model concentrates the entire initial cohort's transmission and then removes
it all at once, producing a sharper and earlier peak. This confirms, more
sharply for larger $\tau$, the point made in the book chapter: the *shape*
of the infectious-period distribution, not merely its mean, drives these
differences.

#### Solution to Exercise 2 {#solution-a01-ex2}

The exercise asks to repeat the two-stage construction for $I(0)=1$ instead
of $10$, confirm conservation and nonnegativity, and check whether a
`ContinuousCallback` that would clamp $I$ to zero ever fires.

```{julia}
#| label: code-sol-a01-ex2
function si_ode!(du, u, p, t)
    S, I = u[1], u[2]
    β, c, _ = p
    λ = β * c * I / (u[1] + u[2] + u[3])
    du[1] = -λ * S
    du[2] = λ * S
    du[3] = 0.0
    return nothing
end

u0_ex2 = [999.0, 1.0, 0.0]
γ = 0.25
p_ex2 = (0.05, 10.0, 1 / γ)

sol_si = solve(ODEProblem(si_ode!, u0_ex2, (0.0, p_ex2[3]), p_ex2), Tsit5();
                reltol = 1e-10, abstol = 1e-10)
history_from_ode(p, t) = sol_si(t)

fire_count = Ref(0)
condition(u, t, integrator) = u[2]                     # zero crossing on I
function affect!(integrator)
    fire_count[] += 1
    integrator.u[2] = max(integrator.u[2], 0.0)
    return nothing
end
cb = ContinuousCallback(condition, affect!; save_positions = (true, true))

prob_dde2 = DDEProblem(sir_dde!, sol_si(p_ex2[3]), history_from_ode, (p_ex2[3], 40.0), p_ex2;
                        constant_lags = [p_ex2[3]])
sol_dde2 = solve(prob_dde2, MethodOfSteps(Tsit5()); reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8, callback = cb)

grid = 0.0:0.1:40.0
states = [t < p_ex2[3] ? sol_si(t) : sol_dde2(t) for t in grid]
conserved = all(u -> isapprox(sum(u), 1000.0; atol = 1e-6), states)
nonnegative = all(u -> all(>=(-1e-8), u), states)
(conserved = conserved, nonnegative = nonnegative, callback_fires = fire_count[])
```

The two-stage construction with $I(0)=1$ still conserves the population and
stays nonnegative, and the clamping callback **never fires**. This is
expected: this DDE is deterministic, and its right-hand side has $I$'s
derivative bounded below by $-\lambda(t-\tau) S(t-\tau) \ge -N$ whenever
$I(t)$ itself is already at $0$ — with an exponential-type solution
structure, $I$ can only approach $0$ asymptotically as the epidemic burns
out, never overshoot below it in finite time. This is in sharp contrast to
the stochastic delay differential equation of the next appendix, whose
diffusion term has no such structural floor and *does* drive $I$ negative
for some seeds, as Exercise 2 there demonstrates concretely.

### Stochastic delay differential equations

#### Solution to Exercise 1 {#solution-a02-ex1}

The exercise asks to repeat the seed-4 run at `dt` $\in \{0.2, 0.1, 0.05\}$,
recording the maximum conservation error and minimum state value, and to
discuss whether decreasing `dt` makes nonnegativity violations more or less
frequent.

```{julia}
#| label: code-sol-a02-ex1
using DelayDiffEq
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using StochasticDiffEq
using SparseArrays
using Random

function sir_dde!(du, u, h, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    β, c, τ = p
    N = S + I + R
    λ = β * c * I / N
    Sd, Id, Rd = h(p, t - τ)
    Nd = Sd + Id + Rd
    λd = β * c * Id / Nd
    du[1] = -λ * S
    du[2] = λ * S - λd * Sd
    du[3] = λd * Sd
    return nothing
end
function sir_delayed_noise!(G, u, h, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    β, c, τ = p
    N = S + I + R
    infection = max(β * c * I / N * S, 0.0)
    Sd, Id, Rd = h(p, t - τ)
    Nd = Sd + Id + Rd
    recovery = max(β * c * Id / Nd * Sd, 0.0)
    G[1, 1] = -sqrt(infection)
    G[2, 1] = sqrt(infection)
    G[2, 2] = -sqrt(recovery)
    G[3, 2] = sqrt(recovery)
    return nothing
end
sir_history(p, t) = [1000.0, 0.0, 0.0]
u0 = [990.0, 10.0, 0.0]
γ = 0.25
p = (0.05, 10.0, 1 / γ)
tspan = (0.0, 40.0)
noise_shape() = sparse([1.0 0.0; 1.0 1.0; 0.0 1.0])

seed4_results = NamedTuple[]
for dt in (0.2, 0.1, 0.05)
    Random.seed!(4)
    prob = SDDEProblem(sir_dde!, sir_delayed_noise!, u0, sir_history, tspan, p;
                        noise_rate_prototype = noise_shape())
    sol = solve(prob, LambaEM(); dt = dt, adaptive = false)
    states = Array(sol)
    push!(seed4_results, (dt = dt,
                           max_conservation_error = round(maximum(abs.(vec(sum(states; dims = 1)) .- 1000.0)); sigdigits = 3),
                           min_state = round(minimum(states); digits = 2)))
end
seed4_results
```

At seed 4 specifically, the minimum state does happen to improve as `dt`
shrinks — but a single seed is not evidence of a general trend, because
changing `dt` under a *fixed* global seed does not refine the *same*
Wiener path; it consumes a different number of Gaussian draws from the RNG
stream and so produces a **different realization altogether**. A fifteen-seed
ensemble at each step size makes this explicit:

```{julia}
#| label: code-sol-a02-ex1-ensemble
ensemble_summary = NamedTuple[]
for dt in (0.2, 0.1, 0.05)
    minvals = Float64[]
    unstable = 0
    for seed in 1:15
        Random.seed!(seed)
        prob = SDDEProblem(sir_dde!, sir_delayed_noise!, u0, sir_history, tspan, p;
                            noise_rate_prototype = noise_shape())
        sol = solve(prob, LambaEM(); dt = dt, adaptive = false)
        if string(sol.retcode) != "Success"
            unstable += 1
            continue
        end
        push!(minvals, minimum(Array(sol)))
    end
    violations = count(<(-1e-6), minvals)
    push!(ensemble_summary, (dt = dt, n_seeds = 15, violations = violations,
                              unstable_runs = unstable,
                              worst_min = round(minimum(minvals); digits = 2)))
end
ensemble_summary
```

Across a fifteen-seed ensemble, the violation *rate* stays roughly constant
(about two-thirds of seeds) at every step size tested, rather than falling
as `dt` shrinks — and at the smallest step size one seed even triggers a
solver instability abort rather than a cleaner trajectory. This is the
opposite of the usual "smaller step, smaller error" relationship from the
calculus and numerical methods unit's convergence study, because that
relationship assumes refining the *same* underlying continuous path. Here,
each `dt` samples an entirely different discretized Wiener process from the
same seed, so nonnegativity — which depends on the specific realized noise
path, not on truncation error — does not improve monotonically with a finer
grid. The only truly reliable statement across step sizes is the structural
one: conservation holds to solver tolerance regardless of `dt`, because it
follows from the noise matrix's construction, not from step-size accuracy.

#### Solution to Exercise 2 {#solution-a02-ex2}

The exercise asks to rerun the seed-1 (caveat) trajectory with a
`DiscreteCallback` that clamps $I$ to zero whenever it is negative, and to
compare the corrected and uncorrected conservation errors.

```{julia}
#| label: code-sol-a02-ex2
Random.seed!(1)
prob_uncorrected = SDDEProblem(sir_dde!, sir_delayed_noise!, u0, sir_history, tspan, p;
                                noise_rate_prototype = noise_shape())
sol_uncorrected = solve(prob_uncorrected, LambaEM(); dt = 0.1, adaptive = false)
states_uncorrected = Array(sol_uncorrected)

fire_count = Ref(0)
clamp_condition(u, t, integrator) = u[2] < 0
function clamp_affect!(integrator)
    fire_count[] += 1
    integrator.u[2] = max(integrator.u[2], 0.0)
    return nothing
end
clamp_cb = DiscreteCallback(clamp_condition, clamp_affect!)

Random.seed!(1)
prob_clamped = SDDEProblem(sir_dde!, sir_delayed_noise!, u0, sir_history, tspan, p;
                            noise_rate_prototype = noise_shape())
sol_clamped = solve(prob_clamped, LambaEM(); dt = 0.1, adaptive = false, callback = clamp_cb)
states_clamped = Array(sol_clamped)

(
    uncorrected_min_I = round(minimum(states_uncorrected[2, :]); digits = 2),
    uncorrected_conservation_error = round(maximum(abs.(vec(sum(states_uncorrected; dims = 1)) .- 1000.0)); sigdigits = 3),
    clamped_min_I = round(minimum(states_clamped[2, :]); digits = 2),
    clamped_conservation_error = round(maximum(abs.(vec(sum(states_clamped; dims = 1)) .- 1000.0)); sigdigits = 3),
    callback_fires = fire_count[],
)
```

The clamp callback fires dozens of times and does raise the minimum value
of $I$ substantially — but it does **not** fully eliminate negative
excursions (the dense interpolation between clamped grid points can still
dip below zero), and, critically, it destroys the *conservation* property
that held to solver tolerance in the uncorrected run: the corrected
trajectory's conservation error is now many orders of magnitude larger than
before. This is the concrete mechanism behind the book chapter's claim that
clamping the current state is an incomplete fix for a **delayed** recovery
term: the clamp only ever touches $I$ at the moment it fires, but the
recovery drift and diffusion at every time $t' \in (t, t+\tau)$ continue to
read the *pre-clamp* history at $t$ through `h(p, t' - \tau)`. Removing mass
from $I$ without removing the corresponding mass from $S$ or $R$ breaks the
$S+I+R=N$ identity, and there is no way to repair that within a single
local correction because the delayed term has already "seen" the
uncorrected value and will keep depending on it for up to $\tau$ more time
units.

### Discrete-event simulation

#### Solution to Exercise 1 {#solution-a03-ex1}

The exercise asks for an `EventQueueABM` recovery event whose `timing`
returns the fixed value $\tau = 1/\gamma = 4$ instead of an exponential
draw, compared against the deterministic DDE at the same parameters.

```{julia}
#| label: code-sol-a03-ex1
using Agents
using Random
using DelayDiffEq
using OrdinaryDiffEq

β = 0.05
c = 10.0
γ = 0.25
N = 1000
I0 = 10
tf = 40.0
τ = 1 / γ

@agent struct QueuePerson(NoSpaceAgent)
    status::Symbol
end

function transmit!(agent, model)
    alter = random_agent(model)
    if alter.status == :I && (rand(abmrng(model)) ≤ model.β)
        agent.status = :I
    end
    return nothing
end
recover!(agent, model) = (agent.status = :R)

transmit_propensity(agent, model) = agent.status == :S ? model.c : 0.0
recovery_propensity(agent, model) = agent.status == :I ? model.γ : 0.0
fixed_delay_timing(agent, model, propensity) = agent.status == :I ? model.τ : Inf

infected(x) = count(==(:I), x)

properties = Dict(:β => β, :c => c, :γ => γ, :τ => τ)
transmit_event = AgentEvent(action! = transmit!, propensity = transmit_propensity)
recovery_event = AgentEvent(action! = recover!, propensity = recovery_propensity, timing = fixed_delay_timing)
model = EventQueueABM(QueuePerson, (transmit_event, recovery_event); properties, rng = Xoshiro(20250711))
for i in 1:N
    add_agent!(QueuePerson(; id = i, status = i <= I0 ? :I : :S), model)
end
data, _ = run!(model, tf; adata = [(:status, infected)])

peak_idx = argmax(data.infected_status)
eq_peak = data.infected_status[peak_idx]
eq_peak_t = data.time[peak_idx]

function sir_dde!(du, u, h, p, t)
    S, I, R = u
    βp, cp, τp = p
    Ntot = S + I + R
    λ = βp * cp * I / Ntot
    Sd, Id, Rd = h(p, t - τp)
    Ntotd = Sd + Id + Rd
    λd = βp * cp * Id / Ntotd
    du[1] = -λ * S
    du[2] = λ * S - λd * Sd
    du[3] = λd * Sd
    return nothing
end
sir_history(p, t) = [1000.0, 0.0, 0.0]
sol_dde = solve(DDEProblem(sir_dde!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], sir_history, (0.0, tf), (β, c, τ);
                            constant_lags = [τ]),
                 MethodOfSteps(Tsit5()); reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-8)
dde_peak, dde_idx = findmax(sol_dde[2, :])

(eq_peak = eq_peak, eq_peak_t = round(eq_peak_t; digits = 2),
 dde_peak = round(dde_peak; digits = 1), dde_peak_t = round(sol_dde.t[dde_idx]; digits = 2))
```

The single stochastic `EventQueueABM` realization peaks close to — a bit
below, as expected for one finite-population sample — the deterministic
DDE's peak, and at a comparable time. This individual-level construction
reaches the same fixed-delay assumption **without a history function**: no
population-level state needs to "remember" what happened $\tau$ time units
ago, because each infectious agent's own scheduled recovery event already
carries that information. The DDE's method of steps is a workaround for the
fact that a population-level ODE has *forgotten* who was infected when; an
individual-level model like this one never has that problem in the first
place.

#### Solution to Exercise 2 {#solution-a03-ex2}

The exercise asks to extend the `ConcurrentSim` model with a `Resource`
representing a limited number of hospital beds, comparing the infectious
curve and wait times against the unconstrained model.

```{julia}
#| label: code-sol-a03-ex2
using ConcurrentSim
using ResumableFunctions
using Distributions

mutable struct BedPerson
    id::Int
    status::Symbol
end
mutable struct BedModel
    sim::Simulation
    β::Float64
    c::Float64
    γ::Float64
    beds::Resource
    Ia::Vector{Int}
    wait_times::Vector{Float64}
    people::Vector{BedPerson}
end

@resumable function live(sim::Simulation, person::BedPerson, m::BedModel, rng)
    while person.status == :S
        @yield timeout(sim, rand(rng, Exponential(1 / m.c)))
        alter = person
        while alter === person
            alter = rand(rng, m.people)
        end
        if alter.status == :I && rand(rng) < m.β
            person.status = :I
            push!(m.Ia, count(pp -> pp.status == :I, m.people))
        end
    end
    if person.status == :I
        request_time = now(sim)
        @yield request(m.beds)
        push!(m.wait_times, now(sim) - request_time)
        @yield timeout(sim, rand(rng, Exponential(1 / m.γ)))
        person.status = :R
        @yield release(m.beds)
        push!(m.Ia, count(pp -> pp.status == :I, m.people))
    end
end

function init_model(S, I, R, β, c, γ, nbeds)
    sim = Simulation()
    beds = Resource(sim, nbeds)
    people = BedPerson[]
    for i in 1:S
        push!(people, BedPerson(i, :S))
    end
    for i in 1:I
        push!(people, BedPerson(S + i, :I))
    end
    for i in 1:R
        push!(people, BedPerson(S + I + i, :R))
    end
    BedModel(sim, β, c, γ, beds, [I], Float64[], people)
end

function run_bed_model(nbeds; seed = 20250711)
    rng = Xoshiro(seed)
    m = init_model(N - I0, I0, 0, β, c, γ, nbeds)
    for person in m.people
        @process live(m.sim, person, m, rng)
    end
    run(m.sim, tf)
    return m
end

unconstrained = run_bed_model(N)     # beds = N: capacity never binds
constrained = run_bed_model(50)

(
    unconstrained_peak_I = maximum(unconstrained.Ia),
    unconstrained_mean_wait = isempty(unconstrained.wait_times) ? 0.0 :
        round(sum(unconstrained.wait_times) / length(unconstrained.wait_times); digits = 2),
    constrained_peak_I = maximum(constrained.Ia),
    constrained_mean_wait = round(sum(constrained.wait_times) / length(constrained.wait_times); digits = 2),
    constrained_max_wait = round(maximum(constrained.wait_times); digits = 2),
    constrained_frac_waited = round(count(>(1e-9), constrained.wait_times) / length(constrained.wait_times); digits = 2),
)
```

With only 50 beds, most infectious individuals wait nearly ten time units on
average (and up to about 26) before a bed frees up — and the epidemic's peak
infectious count is **substantially larger** than in the unconstrained
model, even though $\beta$, $c$, and $\gamma$ are unchanged. The mechanism is
that an individual's `status` is still `:I` (and so can still transmit)
throughout both the *waiting* period and the treatment `timeout`; a scarce
bed supply lengthens the effective time each individual spends counted as
infectious, which is exactly the kind of resource-contention effect a
`Resource` makes easy to express. `EventQueueABM`, as used in this appendix,
has propensities and actions attached to individual agents but no concept
of a shared, capacity-limited object that multiple agents must queue for —
modeling beds there would require encoding the queue and occupancy
bookkeeping by hand inside the agent's own state, which is precisely the
kind of general process/resource abstraction `ConcurrentSim` provides
natively.
